title: Pushed away by a magnet
stem: A bar magnet is brought near object X. X is pushed away. What can you conclude about X?

options.text: X is a magnetic material.
options.pick: Magnetic materials react to magnets, and being pushed away is a reaction.
options.why: Magnetic materials are only ever pulled towards a magnet. They are never pushed away.

options.text: X is a non-magnetic material.
options.pick: Being pushed away feels like “it does not stick”, so it seems not magnetic.
options.why: A non-magnetic material feels no force at all from a magnet. Being pushed is a force.

options.text: X is a magnet.
options.pick: Ask which objects can be pushed away, not just pulled.
options.why: Pushing away is repulsion between like poles, and only two magnets can repel.

options.text: X could be a magnet or a magnetic material; we cannot tell.
options.pick: Both can react to a magnet, so saying we cannot tell feels safest.
options.why: Both are pulled by a magnet, but only a magnet can be pushed away. Repulsion does let us tell.

title: Attracted by both poles
stem: Rod R is attracted to the N pole and to the S pole of a bar magnet, whichever end of R is used. What is R?

options.text: A magnet, because it is attracted by a magnet.
options.pick: Objects that stick to a magnet get called magnets.
options.why: A magnet would be pulled by one pole and pushed by the other, depending on which end faces it. R is never pushed.

options.text: A magnetic material that is not a magnet.
options.pick: Notice that R is pulled by both poles and never pushed by either.
options.why: Always attracted and never repelled is exactly what a magnetic material does.

options.text: A non-magnetic material.
options.pick: It behaves the same way every time, so it seems nothing special is happening.
options.why: A non-magnetic material feels no force. R is attracted, so it is not non-magnetic.

options.text: We cannot tell from attraction alone.
options.pick: Attraction is shared by magnets and magnetic materials, so it seems unreliable.
options.why: Here both poles and both ends were tried. A magnet would have been repelled somewhere, and R never was.

title: Reading a results table
stem: A bar magnet is held near three objects. Each end of the bar magnet is tried. Which row names the objects correctly?
figure:
ObjectNear the N endNear the S end
Pattractedattracted
Qattractedrepelled
Rno forceno force

options.text: P is a magnet; Q is a magnetic material; R is non-magnetic.
options.pick: P is attracted both times, so it looks like the strongest one.
options.why: These are swapped. P is never repelled, so it is a magnetic material. Q is repelled once, so Q is the magnet.

options.text: P is a magnetic material; Q is a magnetic material; R is non-magnetic.
options.pick: P and Q are both attracted at least once, so both look like magnetic materials.
options.why: Q is repelled by the S end. Only a magnet can be repelled, so Q is a magnet.

options.text: P is a magnetic material; Q is a magnet; R is non-magnetic.
options.pick: Use repulsion to pick out the magnet first, then sort the other two.
options.why: Q is the only one repelled, so Q is a magnet. P is only ever attracted, so it is a magnetic material. R feels no force, so it is non-magnetic.

options.text: P is a magnet; Q is a magnet; R is a magnetic material.
options.pick: Any object that reacts at all seems to be a magnet.
options.why: R shows no force at all, so it is non-magnetic, not a magnetic material. P is never repelled, so P is not a magnet.

title: Does resting prove anything?
stem: A toy globe sits on top of a stand and does not move. Ms Tan says, “The stand must be a magnet.” Is she right?

options.text: Yes, because the stand is holding the globe up.
options.pick: Something is keeping the globe in place, so a magnetic hold seems likely.
options.why: Any solid stand holds an object up, magnet or not. Gravity presses the globe onto it.

options.text: Not necessarily. A non-magnetic stand would hold the globe up too, so resting tells us nothing about magnets.
options.pick: Separate what gravity and a solid surface do from what a magnetic force would do.
options.why: Resting is what happens with no magnetic force at all, and also with an attracting force. Only floating shows a push.

options.text: Yes, because the globe stays still.
options.pick: Staying still looks like something is holding it in place by force.
options.why: Objects stay still on a surface without any magnetic force. The stand is simply supporting the globe.

options.text: No, because a magnet would make the globe float.
options.pick: Magnets are the thing that makes toys hover, so a magnet would not let it rest.
options.why: A magnet that attracts the globe makes it cling, not float. Floating needs a push, which needs two magnets with like poles facing.

title: A ball that floats when the base is turned over
stem: A toy has a ball on a base. When the base is turned upside down, the ball floats above it. What can you conclude?

options.text: Only the base is a magnet.
options.pick: The base seems to be the object doing the pushing.
options.why: A ball that is only a magnetic material would be pulled, never pushed. To be pushed away, the ball must be a magnet too.

options.text: Only the ball is a magnet.
options.pick: The ball is the one that moves, so it looks like the magnet.
options.why: A non-magnetic or magnetic-only base cannot push a magnet away. The base must be a magnet as well.

options.text: Both are magnetic materials that are not magnets.
options.pick: Both react to magnets in some way, so calling both “magnetic” feels safe.
options.why: Two magnetic materials show no force on each other, so nothing would make the ball float.

options.text: Both the ball and the base are magnets.
options.pick: Floating means a push, and a push needs two magnets with like poles facing.
options.why: Turned one way, unlike poles face each other and attract, so the ball rests. Turned over, like poles face each other and repel, so the ball floats.
